newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia grenade attack damages democratic hopes.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia grenade attack damages democratic hopes.

text.p: A deadly grenade attack on an opposition rally one week ago has damaged faith in Cambodia's fragile democracy, leaving leaders and donors doubtful peaceful elections will be possible, analysts say.
"There is no more democracy here. We are back to square one," a sombre Sam Rainsy said after four grenades ripped through the opposition leader's demonstration in the Cambodian capital on March 30.
The attack killed 19 people and injured more than 100 and was called the worst act of political violence since Cambodia held historic 1993 elections under the protection of the United Nations.

A week after the explosions turned a routine demonstration in front of the National Assembly into bloody chaos, the streets around the scene are quiet. But few people can muster words more hopeful than those of Sam Rainsy.

"What we saw last Sunday was a litmus test of the strength and movement of democracy in this country, and what you basically see is that this democracy is not getting anywhere. This is very sad," Kao Kim Hourn, director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace think tank, told Reuters.

The implications, said analysts, are that opposition figures have cause to fear they will be silenced, that political rallies may not be tolerated and that a coming election campaign likely will be marred by intimidation and violence.

Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition after Hun Sen rejected his party's loss in the U.N.-sponsored polls of 1993, have already begun squaring off ahead of local and national elections this year and next.
Ranariddh told Reuters he feared last Sunday's attack was the onset of more violence as the bruising campaign unfolds.

Sam Rainsy, a target of the attack along with his fellow demonstrators, blamed the violence directly on co-Premier Hun Sen and reiterated that matters will worsen as he and ally Ranariddh prepare to challenge Hun Sen in the polls together.
Hun Sen has denied involvement and, along with Ranariddh, condemned the attack.
But Hun Sen also suggested the leaders of the demonstration be arrested and be made to accept responsibility for what happened, noting that words can result in bloodshed.
"Do not create arguments which can cause danger to the Cambodian people... A person can make bloodshed for other people with this unreasonable thing," Hun Sen said on Saturday.
Those comments are another bad sign for opposition forces and the electoral process, said human rights observers.
"This is an open policy statement that Hun Sen doesn't believe in open politics. If there can't be (opposition rallies), how can you have a political campaign?" asked one analyst.
In an interview with Reuters, Ranariddh agreed opposition parties and his royalist FUNCINPEC party were in danger, and he was not optimistic about the present state of democracy.
"I think to make this country more democratic, we have to wait for the next election, if (there is) any election.

"Since the attacks on Sunday I think -- I hope -- that the national community and the world community will be aware that it is very, very urgent to do something to save democracy in this country," Ranariddh said.
But what -- or who -- can save Cambodia remains unclear.

The international community is losing patience and hope after spending $3 billion to try to develop democracy in a country still hurt by government infighting, and observers say it is too wary of instability to push the government to reform.

One hope may be the Association of South East Asian Nations -- the regional club expected to admit Cambodia, Burma and Laos later this year. ASEAN diplomats in Cambodia are more optimistic than others and more likely to stay involved in the country.
"Things should become normal again, and hopefully there is enough political will to resolve differences," one diplomat told Reuters.

But if left on its own, Cambodia's fractious coalition may be hard-pressed to recapture the promise of the 1993 polls and move forward to a better place, Sam Rainsy said. "We are in a similar situation as before 1993. The present government is paralyzed."
